(a) 1E1048.1−5937 was detected in the optical and near-infrared during its X-ray flare in 2007; and (b) the mid-infrared emission of this source was not detected by Spitzer, which is consistent with the absence of an infrared excess.
the AXP 1E 1058.1- 5937 has brightened by 1.3–1.6 mag in both the optical and near- infrared during its ongoing X-Ray flare.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the physical properties of the magnetar 1E1048.1 -5937 during an X-ray outburst, using optical and infrared photometric observations and X-ray timing analysis.
the study of the X-ray emission from a sample of 10 X-ray pulsars (XPs), 4 in our Galaxy, 3 in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) and 3 in the Small Magellanic Cloud.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we do not know the origin of the optical and near-infrared flux variations in AXPs, and we cannot rule out either the magnetospheric or disk models.
the optical/near-intrared fluxes of AXPs are variable, but the nature of the variability remains to be understood.
we have no clear idea about the physical origin of the optical/near-intrared flux variations in AXPs.

optical/infrared observations of AXPs are a valuable tool to understand the emission mechanisms of AXPs and their relation to magnetars.
AXPs are highly variable sources in the optical and near-infrared, with the possibility of large amplitude variations on a timescale of years.
